selections.rationale: Every use of this profile needs an identifiable enterprise authority to govern boundary decisions, unresolved risks, exceptions, and profile application across the in-scope AI system.
The pilot adds no United Kingdom-specific enterprise policy content beyond its bounded technical selections; GOV-110 continues to govern the organization's approved AI policy.
Portfolio aggregation and review cadence depend on enterprise portfolio structure rather than the operating-location facts used by this pilot, so no additional profile selection is made.

A named business owner and technical or service owner are necessary for every assessed boundary to attest the United Kingdom operating basis, scope, conditions, resources, and retirement responsibilities.
The profile creates no distinct exception regime or waiver authority; any deviation remains subject to the time-bounded authorization and risk treatment already defined by GOV-140.
Deployment or operation in the United Kingdom does not by itself add a separate enterprise strategy objective or investment priority, so the pilot leaves STR-100 to normal ESAF application.
Value measures and continuation criteria depend on each production capability's intended organizational outcomes, which are not supplied by this jurisdiction profile's technical source boundary.
The approved pilot scope does not add experimentation rules or distinguish research hypotheses; controlled E0 experiments remain governed directly by STR-120 where they occur.
Portfolio resource depth, funding, competencies, and operational capacity are organization-specific planning decisions rather than consequences of the bounded profile conditions.
Every profile assessment needs a consistent risk method to rate, treat, monitor, accept, and escalate the six additional risk lenses without inventing profile-local risk meanings.
Capability classification is required to define the assessed boundary and interpret exposure, data sensitivity, external dependency, criticality, and uncertainty for every in-scope AI system.
Each unresolved profile risk and condition-driven safeguard needs documented treatment, monitoring, and accountable residual-risk acceptance before continued operation within the declared boundary.
Impact-assessment depth is tied to E2 through E4 capability characteristics and affected parties, not to a universal fact established by this technical jurisdiction pilot.
Material-change reassessment remains an underlying lifecycle obligation, but the pilot does not add a separate change trigger beyond the condition and evidence refresh requirements it states.
Complete human, service, workload, API, agent, and third-party identity coverage is necessary to reconcile access and administration to every assessed system boundary.

Every in-scope system has non-public assets or administrative functions whose identities must be authenticated with risk-proportionate mechanisms, including systems that expose public service endpoints.
Purpose-bound authorization and least privilege are universal foundations for limiting access to models, data, prompts, tools, integrations, and administrative actions in the assessed boundary.

Every assessed AI boundary includes privileged functions capable of changing configuration, data, models, instructions, logs, or policy, so their stronger authentication, restriction, and monitoring are selected.
Third-party administration creates an additional need to govern the credentials, tokens, and keys used across external support paths and to verify prompt, code, log, and documentation handling.
Access inventories used by this profile must be periodically reviewed and promptly corrected when purpose, role, employment, authorization, supplier relationship, or operational need changes.
Data authority and permitted purpose depend on each dataset, contract, and processing context; the profile's deployment location alone supplies no additional authority or use permission.

The assessed boundary cannot support reliable access, logging, sharing, retention, or protection decisions unless prompts, outputs, embeddings, telemetry, and other AI data are classified and handled.
Accuracy, representativeness, timeliness, and fitness criteria must be derived from the capability's intended use and data population, which this technical profile does not define.
The pilot does not add a profile-specific lineage granularity or reproducibility rule; material data provenance remains governed by DAT-130 according to risk and obligations.
Personal-data processing is not established for every in-scope system, and interpreting privacy duties is outside the approved source boundary, so no profile selection is added.
Retrieval, embedding, vector search, and long-term memory are capability facts not represented by the bounded pilot conditions; their protections remain governed by DAT-150 when present.
Output and feedback handling must follow actual content, intended use, reliability, intellectual-property status, and downstream impact rather than a universal jurisdiction-profile rule.

Every assessed AI system depends on one or more identifiable models, so complete ownership, version, provider, validation, deployment, review, and retirement records are required for boundary coverage.

When a model can enter approved use through an untrusted intake path, its source, licensing, usage rights, integrity, dependencies, limitations, supplier terms, and modification history require verification.

Model validation criteria must be tailored to intended performance, safety, fairness, privacy, robustness, and operating conditions; this infrastructure-focused pilot does not define those use-specific thresholds.
The pilot adds no separate provider-version or model-release process; model changes continue to require the authorization, testing, monitoring, and rollback defined by MOD-130.
Protection depth for weights, parameters, configurations, and restricted interfaces depends on the model deployment and sensitivity, not solely on the approved profile conditions.
A model that is end-of-life, replaced, unsupported, compromised, nonconforming, expired, or abandoned requires an authorized retirement path that removes deployment and access and verifies closure.
Every in-scope AI application needs documented trust boundaries, flows, threats, failure modes, oversight points, and validation criteria to establish the technical boundary used by this profile.

Instruction, user-input, retrieval, tool-output, and memory protections depend on the application's actual context channels; the bounded profile conditions do not establish those channels universally.
Output validation and authorization must reflect each destination, action, uncertainty, and impact, so this jurisdiction package does not add a generic profile-level selection.
Tenant, session, cache, conversation, and memory isolation requirements depend on application state and tenancy architecture, which are not resolved by this pilot's conditions.

When untrusted artifacts can enter an internally built or materially configured AI application or pipeline, its code, prompts, workflows, dependencies, builds, releases, vulnerabilities, and changes require controlled assurance.

Internet reachability materially increases automated abuse, denial-of-service, consumption, adversarial behavior, and policy-evasion opportunities at AI application interfaces, activating dedicated misuse controls.
Gateway architecture is not universal because equivalent policy enforcement may exist elsewhere and the control applies to production service access; the profile does not prescribe one topology.

Internet-reachable AI, management, tool, callback, streaming, or batch interfaces require explicit authentication, authorization, validation, encryption, limits, versioning, logging, monitoring, and secure deprecation.

When the AI capability can invoke a tool or plugin, every callable function, connector, action, script, browser, code facility, database, or business integration requires governed inventory and constraints.
MCP or comparable orchestration is not present in every AI system and no bounded condition establishes it, so the pilot makes no additional orchestration-security selection.
External provider use requires service-specific security, privacy, data-use, retention, availability, change, incident, assurance, continuity, and exit expectations for the integration.

An E1 through E4 capability with a material external provider or platform dependency requires documented and tested interfaces, formats, configuration, migration procedures, and exit criteria proportionate to continuity and concentration risk.
Every in-scope workload, model, dataset, and supporting service must reside in an environment approved for its risk, classification, architecture, jurisdiction, isolation, assurance, and operations.

A versioned hardening baseline is necessary for the compute, hosts, containers, networks, storage, runtimes, and management interfaces supporting every declared AI boundary, including inherited responsibilities.

Internet exposure, untrusted infrastructure-dependency intake, or an unsupported infrastructure component establishes a concrete vulnerability context for hosts, firmware, drivers, containers, orchestration, model servers, libraries, storage, networks, or managed services.
Reproducible, reviewed, tested, approved, monitored, and recoverable configuration is required to reconcile the actual infrastructure state and material changes for every assessed boundary.

Internet-reachable services and administrative paths require approved cryptographic mechanisms and key management for communications, credentials, data, models, backups, and management traffic according to risk.

Internet reachability increases automated demand, denial-of-service, uncontrolled-consumption, and harmful-contention risk, requiring capacity, quota, isolation, priority, budget, concurrency, scaling, and shutdown safeguards proportionate to the exposed service.
Agent presence is not established by the bounded profile conditions, so the pilot adds no agent-identity selection while AGT-100 continues to govern any agents actually deployed.
Data, tool, target, action, delegation, and side-effect permissions are agent-specific architecture facts that cannot be inferred from United Kingdom operation or the selected technical conditions.
Human approval and intervention requirements must reflect agent action impact, reversibility, uncertainty, affected parties, and safety consequences, none of which this pilot resolves universally.
Agent memory and state are not universal system components, and the profile conditions do not establish their purpose, tenant, sensitivity, source, retention, or deletion needs.
Agent instruction, plan, tool-call, permission, approval, action, and outcome traceability applies when agents act; the pilot does not add a separate agent-capability condition.
Pause, restriction, isolation, termination, rollback, recovery, and safe-resume mechanisms depend on an agent deployment and its action risks, which are outside the bounded condition catalog.
Multi-agent communication, delegation, shared state, conflict, termination, and emergent behavior cannot be assumed for all systems deployed or operated within the profile scope.
Service objectives apply to E1 through E4 production capabilities and shared platforms; the profile also covers non-production systems and does not define capability-specific service targets.
The pilot adds evidence refresh expectations but no distinct release taxonomy or approval workflow; AI changes remain governed by OPS-110 according to impact and dependencies.
Incident preparation and response remain essential ESAF obligations, but the pilot does not define a separate jurisdiction-specific incident category, communication path, or reporting rule.
Continuity, fallback, recovery, and provider-failure arrangements depend on E1 through E4 criticality, substitutability, and failure consequence, which this profile does not determine.
Availability, latency, throughput, quality, utilization, demand, and cost objectives are production-service facts not established across all systems in this jurisdiction profile.

When accountable authority determines that an experiment, pilot, production service, embedded capability, or third-party AI service must retire, its users, dependencies, access, suppliers, records, continuity, and decommissioning require an approved process.

Every assessed boundary needs attributable, time-synchronized, protected telemetry sufficient to connect identity, configuration, performance, policy, cost, and relevant AI events to assessment evidence.

Internet reachability activates focused detection and investigation for unauthorized access, prompt or context attacks, data exposure, model abuse, extraction, policy evasion, and anomalous consumption.

Production behavior baselines for performance, drift, safety, fairness, reliability, and uncertainty depend on capability purpose and feedback availability rather than this profile's infrastructure conditions.
Agent monitoring applies only when agents exist, and no selected condition establishes agent identity, plans, delegation, memory, interventions, or outcome monitoring for the assessed system.
Alert ownership, priorities, service levels, containment, and tuning must reflect actual monitoring design and risk; the profile adds no universal alert-response operating model.

Protected, attributable audit trails for access, configuration, privileged activity, model and data changes, incidents, and governance decisions are necessary to reconstruct every profile assessment boundary.
Identifying and interpreting applicable obligations requires authorities beyond the approved source boundary; this profile therefore adds no legal, regulatory, contractual, or sector interpretation.
Record, notice, registration, disclosure, and reporting duties depend on applicable authorities and audiences not defined by this pilot, so CMP-110 remains directly applicable as appropriate.

External providers or administrators require assigned and verified third-party responsibilities for security, data use, change, incidents, assurance, continuity, subcontractors, privileged support, and exit.

The pilot establishes its own operating-location applicability but does not interpret residency, transfer, government-access, geographic-support, sovereignty, contract, or customer requirements for particular data or services.
Ownership, licensing, attribution, distribution, training, output, indemnity, and restriction requirements depend on the actual acquired or generated assets, which the profile does not specify.

Assessment-program frequency, sampling, independence, reporting, and follow-up are enterprise assurance decisions; the pilot defines package evidence expectations but not a replacement assessment program.
Assessor competence and independence must match each technical, governance, privacy, safety, compliance, or control subject; the profile cannot set one universal personnel threshold.

Every profile conclusion must rest on relevant, reliable, complete, timely, attributable, integrity-protected evidence sufficient for its procedure, determination, declared scope, and assessment period.
Finding severity, remediation priority, due date, retest, closure, and acceptance remain governed by the assessed risk and root cause rather than a jurisdiction-profile-specific disposition process.
Management-review cadence and portfolio inputs concern the enterprise AI management system as a whole; this pilot adds no separate executive review body or schedule.
Baseline literacy remains an enterprise requirement, but the infrastructure and evidence conditions in this pilot do not add a distinct curriculum for all personnel affected by AI.
Role-based competency must be defined for actual design, validation, operation, security, governance, audit, and use responsibilities, which the profile's technical facts do not enumerate.
Acceptable-use education depends on the organization's approved services, data boundaries, user actions, and policy; the pilot does not create additional user-access training content.
Secure engineering training applies to personnel performing defined development and maintenance work, but the profile conditions do not establish those roles across every in-scope system.
Executive and governance education must reflect assigned authority, risk acceptance, review, and audit duties; this package adds no profile-local competency or education schedule.
Architecture governance remains necessary for new capabilities, changes, shared platforms, exceptions, and retirement, but the pilot adds no separate pattern approval or technical-debt process.

Documented components, actors, identities, flows, trust levels, dependencies, administrative paths, and enforcement boundaries are indispensable to define and evidence every system assessed with this profile.
Reusable reference patterns depend on recurring organizational architectures and governance maturity; this first jurisdiction pilot does not require a particular pattern library or deviation process.
Failure design applies to E1 through E4 based on consequence, criticality, and substitutability; the pilot's conditions do not establish one resilience design for all systems.

External provider use or third-party administration requires documented, approved, validated, and monitored responsibility boundaries for inherited controls, service outcomes, evidence access, and administrative paths.

Unsupported components require governed currency, compatibility, technical-debt, support, replacement, deprecation, and retirement decisions across models, runtimes, protocols, platforms, tools, interfaces, and infrastructure.
